The foundational principle linking communication and governance is that effective state formation depends on scalable information transfer. Primitive communities are constrained by language transmission delays, limiting their size to several million individuals. This constraint arises from the combinatorial explosion of inter-agent communication required for coordinated action. Empires like Persia and Rome overcame this by building infrastructures—roads, relay systems—that enabled rapid dissemination of directives. Modern communication technologies such as aviation and radio have effectively eliminated these constraints, enabling global-scale coordination. The resulting system exhibits emergent properties where state boundaries become fluid, and sovereignty is increasingly mediated through information flows rather than territorial control. The mathematical model underlying this is a feedback loop between information throughput and organizational resilience, governed by entropy-based measures of coherence. Failure modes include breakdowns in communication channels leading to cascading inefficiencies and loss of collective agency.
